summary: ARES OUTPOST is a browser-based 3D survival game that puts students in charge of a one-person outpost in Mars' Jezero Crater region. To stay alive, players must constantly balance the same trade-offs real mission planners face: suit oxygen, body temperature, radiation dose, power, water and food. They mine iron ore and water ice, melt ice into drinking water, craft O₂ canisters and heat packs, build a greenhouse to grow potatoes and a pressurized rover, and race back to shelter when dust storms or solar particle events hit. Every choice has a cost: sprinting burns oxygen faster, nights drop to -80°C, and staying outside during a solar storm can be fatal. A remote-controlled car and a scouting drone with ground-penetrating radar let players explore and locate buried iron deposits. By turning abstract engineering trade-offs into tangible, moment-to-moment decisions, the game lets young learners experience firsthand why life support, shielding, power and food production decide whether a mission succeeds or fails. Key values and systems, such as Mars gravity, the surface radiation dose measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument and the habitat's MOXIE-style oxygen generator, are based on NASA sources. It runs instantly in any modern browser with no installation.
details:
What it does

ARES OUTPOST is a first-person 3D Mars survival simulation built as a junior astronaut mission trainer. The player is an astronaut alone at a small outpost in the Jezero Crater region and has to keep both themselves and the base alive. The game does not explain trade-offs in text; it makes students live them. Every system competes for the same limited resources, so each decision (go out now or wait, build the greenhouse or the rover first, keep exploring or head back) has visible consequences.

How it works: the trade-offs players manage

  • Life support: The suit's O₂ tank drains continuously and faster while sprinting or mining. It refills only inside the pressurized habitat, which is entered through a two-door airlock that has to pressurize and depressurize.
  • Thermal control: Body temperature follows the outside temperature, from about -18°C around midday to -82°C at night. Heat packs, the heated habitat, rover cabin and greenhouse keep the astronaut warm.
  • Radiation shielding: Dose builds up from galactic cosmic rays (the baseline of about 28 µSv/h matches Curiosity RAD's 0.67 mSv/day surface measurement), rises during the day and spikes during solar particle events. The habitat fully shields, the greenhouse blocks about 60% and the rover about 50%, so where you are matters.
  • Water and food: Hydration and nutrition drop over time. Players mine water ice, which the habitat's melter turns into filtered water for the tank (1 kg ice gives 0.9 L). Potatoes grown in the greenhouse provide food, but the plants also consume irrigation water from the same tank.
  • Power and mobility: The pressurized rover runs on a battery that drains while driving and recharges from solar panels and the base dock. Its cabin has its own O₂ reserve.
  • Resources and construction: Iron comes from hematite ore, rare iron-nickel meteorites and buried deposits dug out with tools. Iron and water are spent on the greenhouse (16 kg iron + 10 L water), the rover (24 kg iron + 5 L water), O₂ canisters, heat packs and tools (shovel, pickaxe, cutting sword, drill), which wear out with use.
  • Remote exploration: A remote-controlled car with a limited 150 m signal range carries a scouting drone. The drone's ground-penetrating radar scan, inspired by Perseverance's RIMFAX instrument, marks buried iron deposits on the compass.
  • Hazards: Dust storms reduce visibility and temperature, solar particle events give a short warning before a radiation spike, and falls can hurt even in 0.38 g.
  • Learning from failure: When the mission fails, the game shows the exact cause (hypoxia, hypothermia, acute radiation syndrome, dehydration or starvation) together with the player's statistics, so students can reflect and try a better strategy.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Makes abstract mission engineering trade-offs (life support, shielding, power, food production) tangible and fun for young learners.
  • Lets students fail safely and learn by trying again, the same way real mission planning works.
  • Teaches real Mars science along the way: low gravity, extreme cold, a thin atmosphere, radiation, dust storms, water ice, hematite, the butterscotch daytime sky and blue sunsets, and the orbits of Phobos and Deimos.
  • Runs instantly in any modern browser on school computers, with no installation, account or cost.

Tools and technologies

  • JavaScript (ES modules), HTML5 and CSS3, with no build step and no backend.
  • Three.js (WebGL) for 3D rendering, with a fixed-timestep physics loop and interpolated rendering.
  • Procedurally generated terrain (craters, layered mesas, dark basalt dunes, boulders) and procedural textures, so no large asset downloads are needed.
  • Hosted on Vercel as a static website.

Creativity and design choices

  • Combines a survival-game loop with real mission systems: an airlock state machine, a habitat ice melter and water tank, a greenhouse, a pressurized rover, tool durability, and an RC car plus drone that let players explore without risking the astronaut.
  • A helmet visor HUD with frost, hypoxia and damage effects makes the astronaut's condition easy to read at a glance.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy vs. playability: We kept real values where they matter (Mars gravity of 3.72 m/s², night temperatures around -80°C, the RAD surface dose, a MOXIE-style oxygen generator in the habitat, Jezero Crater as the setting) and compressed time for pacing (one sol lasts 8 minutes and a full suit tank about 5 minutes).
  • Age-appropriate difficulty: Clear on-screen prompts, warnings and notifications guide the player without hiding the consequences of their choices.
  • Accessibility and performance: Lightweight, browser-based and tuned to run on ordinary school hardware.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) tools

We used SI tools (large language models and AI coding assistants such as Claude and Claude Code) throughout the project: for ideation and brainstorming, researching Mars and NASA mission facts, data interpretation, writing and debugging the game code, writing, editing and translating the in-game text and this submission, visual design, and preparing our demo video. All SI-assisted code and content was reviewed, tested and refined by our team. No NASA logos or other NASA branding elements are used in the game.
